tier_reason: First-party README tables compare bigfft with Go math/big (and GMP) and name the CPUs (Core 2 Quad Q8200, Core i5-4590), but give no Go version or build settings; benchmark code exists only as the repo's Go test files, so the evidence falls short of A.

corrections.caveats: The author calls it 'a toy proof-of-concept implementation' of Schonhage-Strassen, not meant for production. It does not beat GMP: the README's GMP table shows GMP about 1.2x to 3.1x faster at every size (derived from page data: bigfft ns/op divided by GMP ns/op). Versus Go's math/big it only wins above roughly 1 Mbit (FFT switches on above 200 kbits; at 1 kb to 100 kb it is up to 4.9% slower), and decimal scanning is slower up to 1e4 digits. Old CPUs; Go version unstated; last commit 2023-01-29. Go library, not callable from C++ without cgo glue.

notes: All quoted numbers match the README (math/big table, GMP table, decimal-scan table). Metadata confirmed on github.com: BSD-3-Clause, 92 stars, 20 forks, not fork/archived, last commit 2023-01-29 (abandoned by the >3-year rule).

tier_reason: The only numbers are one first-party README sentence (272 ms vs 530 ms for fib(100,000)) with no hardware, compiler, build mode or comparison code; Sources/Benchmarks/Benchmarks.swift only times BInt itself against a saved BInt baseline and contains no GMP or mini-gmp code.

corrections.baseline: mini-gmp (GMP's portable minimal subset without assembly kernels); the README says full GMP was not counted because it needs to be installed and is not portable
corrections.claimed_speedup: README 'About performance': 'BInt about twice as fast as mini-gmp, as of now (not counting the normal gmp, because it needs to be installed and is not portable). For example, BInt can add numbers about 2 times faster than GMP (272ms vs 530ms for fib(100,000)), and multiplication is more than twice as fast. When given the task of calculating and printing factorials successively, BInt performs significantly better than GMP.' In context 'GMP' in the later sentences refers to the mini-gmp comparison; no comparison with full GMP is claimed.
corrections.workload: README claim: fib(100,000) via big-integer addition, multiplication, and successive factorials with printing, BInt vs mini-gmp. The repo's Sources/Benchmarks (Benchmarks.swift, main.swift) time BInt-only workloads (factorial of 40,000, Fib 100000, 10^300000, matrix power, Mersenne search) for regression comparison and contain no GMP or mini-gmp code.
corrections.caveats: The baseline is mini-gmp, not full GMP (the README explicitly excludes normal GMP), so this is not a GMP-beater. First-party README sentence only: no hardware, compiler, build configuration, date or comparison code; the README notes release builds run more than 10x faster than Xcode debug builds. Swift library, not callable from C++ directly.

tier_reason: First-party README benchmark tables (u256 vs big.Int time/op, B/op, allocs/op) with the go test -bench commands, but no CPU model, Go version or date for the tables, so short of A.

corrections.caveats: Baseline is Go's math/big, not GMP or MPFR, so baseline_in_list is false; included as the incumbent for Go big-integer use. The README gives the benchmark commands (go test -run - -bench . -benchmem) but no CPU model or Go version for the tables; the only date is 'As of 2020-03-18' in the status line. The 'orders of magnitude' wording is not borne out by the tables: the largest gain is Exp/small at -94.21% (about 17x), and some rows are small (MulMod/mod64 -18.60%, Decimal/ToDecimal -19.23%). Fixed-width versus arbitrary-width comparison favors the specialised type. Go library, not callable from C++ directly.
